passage:
Dear Dilnaz,
You asked how I stayed so calm last week. Honestly, I wasn't calm, I was curious about how little I cared. A stranger kept replying under my cooking videos with the same insult, only to watch me react. Old me would have typed a paragraph. This time I muted, blocked, and went to make tea. The next day a different person wrote, politely, that my rice timings were off for old cookers. That one I answered, with thanks. Ignoring the first wasn't weakness; it kept my evenings mine. The troll got nothing from me, and I had forgotten the name by dinner 🙂
Come on Sunday and taste the corrected rice.
Zeenat

qa.q: Which stranger did Zeenat answer, and what had that person pointed out?
qa.a: Zeenat answered the one who wrote, politely, that the rice timings were off for old cookers, and replied with thanks.

qa.q: What does Zeenat mean by saying that ignoring the first stranger wasn't weakness?
qa.a: Zeenat sees ignoring the troll as protection. It kept the evenings calm and gave the person who only wanted a reaction nothing.

qa.q: How can Dilnaz tell which comments deserve a reply?
qa.a: Answer people who criticise in good faith, like the rice-timing comment, and mute or block those who only want a reaction.

qa.q: What was the troll probably after, and what happened instead?
qa.a: They wanted to watch Zeenat react and get attention. After the mute and block they got no reaction at all.

grounding: A troll provokes for attention; not feeding them by muting and blocking is protection, while good-faith criticism gets an answer.

passage: Late evening in the hostel common room, Avni noticed Kashish's chair empty for the third night. Kashish's post about a college cricket match had been picked up by strangers who mocked her all day, and her door stayed shut. Avni did not knock with advice. She sent a private message: "No need to answer. I'm here. What would help right now? I can read the comments so you don't have to." An hour later a reply came: "Could you just sit with me?" Avni brought two cups of tea and sat on the floor by the bed, saying almost nothing. She resisted the urge to post a defence under the thread. Near midnight Kashish said, "Thanks for not fixing it."

qa.q: What did Avni offer to do with the comments?
qa.a: She offered to read the comments so Kashish wouldn't have to.

qa.q: Why did Avni hold back from posting a defence under the thread?
qa.a: Avni felt protective of Kashish but held back, sensing that quiet presence would help more than adding public noise to the mocking thread.

qa.q: What else could Avni do over the next few days to support Kashish?
qa.a: Keep asking what would help, offer again to check the messages, and stay nearby without pushing advice.

qa.q: What might Kashish have meant by "Thanks for not fixing it"?
qa.a: Kashish was probably relieved to be listened to without advice. Company felt more helpful than solutions while sinking under the mockery.

grounding: A friend is being trolled and sinking; a private message, asking what help is wanted, offering to read messages and just being present.

passage: Two weeks ago I posted a joke about how people from Ojas's hometown talk. I thought it was harmless. It wasn't. Replies piled up, and one was from Ojas, short and quiet: "That one stung." My first instinct was to write, "It was only a joke, people are too sensitive." I typed it, then looked at it for a long time. Instead I deleted the joke and called Ojas that evening. I said I was sorry, that I had laughed at something I never bothered to understand, and that I had no excuse. I asked what I could do. Ojas said listening was enough for now. I've stopped making jokes like that, and I'm still learning why they landed the way they did. — Harish

qa.q: What did Ojas reply under Harish's joke?
qa.a: Ojas wrote, "That one stung."

qa.q: Why did Harish look for a long time at the reply Harish had typed, instead of posting it?
qa.a: Harish seemed to realise that "It was only a joke" was a defensive excuse that would brush aside Ojas's hurt.

qa.q: What could Harish do to keep repairing things after the apology?
qa.a: Keep listening, stay away from jokes like that, keep learning why they hurt, and apologise to anyone else who was harmed.

qa.q: How might Ojas have felt when Harish phoned with no excuses?
qa.a: Ojas was hurt at first, and probably felt heard. Saying listening was enough "for now" suggests trust is mending slowly, not all at once.

grounding: A careless post hurts someone; Harish drops the defensive reply, apologises directly, and changes behaviour.

passage:
Indu: Payal!! Uncle just forwarded a video. A bridge collapsing in our city, people screaming 😰
Indu: I'm about to send it to the college group
Payal: wait. where's it from?
Indu: no source, just "share fast"
Payal: check the date and see if any news site has it
Indu: ...reverse search says it's from another country, three years ago
Indu: my heart was racing for nothing 😅
Payal: that's the point of those, they want you shaking
Indu: I'll message Uncle privately with the link. Not in the family group
Later:
Indu: Sent. He replied "oh, I didn't know, thanks beta"
Payal: kind of you 🙂

qa.q: Where did Indu's search show the video was from?
qa.a: It showed the video was from another country, three years ago.

qa.q: Why was Indu's heart racing, and what did it turn out to be?
qa.a: Indu was frightened by the shocking bridge video. The racing was for nothing, since the clip was old and from elsewhere.

qa.q: What should Indu do next time a shocking video arrives before sharing it?
qa.a: Pause and check the source, the date and independent reports, remembering that strong emotion is itself a warning, and correct the sender privately with a link.

qa.q: How might Uncle have felt getting Indu's private message?
qa.a: Probably not embarrassed, since it was private and polite. His reply, "oh, I didn't know, thanks beta," sounds thankful.

grounding: An uncle forwards a shocking video; Indu pauses, checks source and date, and corrects the uncle gently in private with a link.

passage: Ankita played the audio for the third time at her desk. It sounded exactly like the bank's regional head announcing that customers' savings would be frozen on Friday. Her chest tightened, and she was already drafting a message to her parents. Jyoti, at the next desk, leaned over. "Play it again, but watch the video." The lips slid slightly out of step with the words, and the speaker hardly blinked. There was nothing about it on the bank's official website or in the morning papers. Jyoti suggested calling the helpline printed on Ankita's card, and the officer said it was a fake going around that day. Ankita covered her face and laughed shakily. "I feel so stupid." "It was made to be believed," Jyoti said. "That's what they're for."

qa.q: What did the fake announcement say would happen on Friday?
qa.a: It said customers' savings would be frozen on Friday.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she said "I feel so stupid"?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and shaken at having been fooled, as the shaky laugh and covered face show.

qa.q: How can someone check a startling clip like this?
qa.a: Watch for lips out of step with the words and little blinking, look for coverage on the official website or in reliable papers, and ask the official helpline.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see Ankita being taken in?
qa.a: As understandable, not foolish. Jyoti says the clip "was made to be believed."

grounding: A fake clip copies a real person; signs like odd lip sync, no blinking or no reliable coverage, verification through official channels, and no shame in being tricked.

passage:
Subject: Something I need you to know
Dear Urmila,
Yesterday someone sent me a video that puts my face into a scene I was never in, and it has already reached people from work. Then came a message asking for money to stop it going further. My hands shook for an hour, and part of me wanted to hide. But I keep telling myself this: someone violated me, and the shame is not mine. I saved every message and the link, reported the video to the platform and the cybercrime portal, and told my parents and one friend. I'm meeting a lawyer on Thursday. I am not paying anything. Could you call me tonight? I'd like to hear a familiar voice.
Sumit

qa.q: What did the message that came after the video ask for?
qa.a: It asked for money to stop the video going further.

qa.q: Why does Sumit insist that the shame is not Sumit's own?
qa.a: Sumit was never in that scene, so the wrong belongs to whoever made and sent it. Part of Sumit wanted to hide, and the reminder pushes back on that shame.

qa.q: What should Sumit keep doing if more demands arrive?
qa.a: Not pay, keep saving evidence, keep reporting, and lean on trusted people and the lawyer.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel on receiving this email?
qa.a: Probably worried and also trusted, since Sumit chose to confide. Sumit asks for a call, so listening without judging is what would help. 🤍

grounding: A fake video spreads: a violation, not shame; saving evidence, reporting to platform and cybercrime portal, telling trusted people, seeing a lawyer, refusing to pay.

passage: A jeep with a loudspeaker stopped at the village chowk, and Chetan, sharing a bench with the old men, heard a clip of the rival candidate saying the water tank would be sold off. His stomach clenched. He thought of his mother filling pots at dawn. By evening the clip was on every phone. Leela, who ran the seed shop, frowned at it. "It cuts off mid-sentence," she said. "Who gains if we're scared?" She listened to the full speech on the radio with Chetan, and the candidate had said the opposite. They walked to the block office, where a notice showed the tank was not being sold. "The candidate I like has flattering clips too," Leela added. "I check those as well."

qa.q: What did the clip claim would happen to the water tank?
qa.a: It claimed the water tank would be sold off.

qa.q: Why did Chetan's stomach clench when he heard the clip?
qa.a: He was afraid of losing the water, and he pictured his mother filling pots at dawn.

qa.q: Which steps helped Chetan and Leela find out the truth?
qa.a: They noticed the clip cut off mid-sentence, asked who gains from fear, listened to the full speech on the radio and checked the notice at the block office.

qa.q: How does Leela see clips that flatter her own side?
qa.a: She is wary of them too, and checks them as well.

grounding: Campaign clips and fear rumours steer emotion; Chetan learns to ask who benefits and check several sources, even for flattering content.

passage:
"Neelam, you can't seriously think the moon landing was staged."
"Gargi, look at the flag. It waves. There's no air up there."
"Hold on." Gargi put down her chai. "Where did you first see that? I'm curious how you got there."
"A long video my cousin sent. It made a lot of sense."
"Okay. Can I tell you just one thing? The flag had a rod sewn along the top so it stayed out. It looked like waving because they twisted the pole."
"Huh." Neelam frowned. "Nobody mentioned the rod."
"I'm not saying your cousin is silly. It's a clever video. Send it to me? I'll watch it properly."
"Fine 🙂 But I'm not promising to change my mind."
"Deal. More chai?"

qa.q: What did Neelam point to as proof that the moon landing was staged?
qa.a: Neelam pointed to the flag, which waves although there is no air up there.

qa.q: Why did Gargi ask where Neelam first saw the claim, instead of just saying it was wrong?
qa.a: Gargi was curious about how Neelam got there and wanted to respect a friend rather than humiliate, since people rarely change when they feel attacked.

qa.q: What could Gargi do if Neelam still isn't convinced later?
qa.a: Stay friendly, share another single fact when it fits, and keep watching the cousin's video together rather than arguing harder.

qa.q: How does Neelam seem to take Gargi's approach?
qa.a: Neelam did not feel attacked. Agreeing to send the video, while saying no promise to change, shows a friend still honest and at ease.

grounding: A friend holds a conspiracy theory; Gargi asks how they came to it, shares one reliable fact and avoids humiliating them.

qa.q: How was Aditi feeling when Ishita said Mr Gupta's shop had been mobbed?
qa.a: Aditi felt sick and guilty, and moved straight to delete the message.

qa.q: What did Aditi do to repair the harm, and what would help in future?

grounding: Sharing a false message causes panic and hurts someone named; delete, correct to the same audience, apologise, and check before sharing.

passage:
Dear Jahnavi,
You asked why I've gone quiet on the group chat. I had been reading my feed for hours, angry at strangers, and I noticed I'd become sharp with everyone, even you. My views were getting stranger too, and everything felt like an emergency. Then I remembered what you said: outrage is what these platforms reward. So I cut my feed down to a few sources I trust, put my phone in the drawer after nine, and started a long book about rivers of all things. Two weeks in, I sleep better and argue less. I'm shaping my mind with whatever I pay attention to. Come over on Saturday and tell me which of my old takes were nonsense 🙂
Akash

qa.q: What does Akash do with the phone after nine?
qa.a: Akash puts the phone in the drawer after nine.

qa.q: How did Akash feel before changing habits, and what did Akash notice?
qa.a: Akash had felt angry and on edge after hours on the feed, becoming sharp with everyone while views got stranger and everything felt like an emergency.

qa.q: What else could Akash try if the anger creeps back?
qa.a: Keep the short list of trusted sources, keep the offline time and the long reading, and talk it over with Jahnavi.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Akash's change?
qa.a: Jahnavi may be glad that the remark about outrage landed. The invitation to point out nonsense suggests Akash is open to honest feedback.

grounding: A feed keeps you angry and hooked; curating sources, scheduling offline time, reading long-form, and remembering outrage is rewarded.
